description: We’re Pyronauts, the team behind FlameFall. We turn NASA’s combustion experiments into evidence you can explore, compare, and trace back to the source. Our first question takes us from an acrylic flame on the ISS to a lunar rover.
summary: Flame Fall helps spacecraft fire-safety researchers answer a question that matters for every new mission: Which NASA fire experiments apply to the conditions we’ll actually fly in? Built for the Flame in Freefall challenge, our interactive dashboard ranks relevant studies, lets users compare individual tests, and links findings to the original NASA records. In one walkthrough, users move from an acrylic combustion test aboard the International Space Station to a proposed lunar rover environment and see where differences in gravity, oxygen, pressure, and airflow leave open questions. By showing what NASA has tested and which conditions still need evidence, Flame Fall helps researchers decide what to test next as they design for crew safety beyond Earth.
details:
Flame Fall

You’re designing ventilation for a crewed lunar rover. NASA has burned acrylic on the ISS and tested it under simulated lunar gravity. Which results apply to your rover, and what would you test next?

We built Flame Fall for NASA’s Flame in Freefall challenge to make that question answerable with evidence. It’s an interactive dashboard that lets students and researchers start with a mission scenario, find the experiments that speak to it, and see where the data leave an open question.

From mission question to experiment

Enter a research question, try the ISS or lunar rover preset, or set your own conditions. Flame Fall ranks five investigations across material flammability, ventilation, fire spread, smoke detection, and suppression. Each result explains why it surfaced and links to the original report, table, or figure.

In the demo, you can compare two verified BASS-II acrylic burn runs, then step through a five-stage airflow sequence documented by NASA. Switch to the lunar rover preset and check gravity, oxygen, pressure, and airflow against the evidence. The dashboard shows which conditions have individual matches and whether either verified run tested them together. You can download the curated run and phase data with a data dictionary and source manifest. To address the gap, we’d measure acrylic flame spread at simulated lunar gravity under the rover’s target oxygen concentration and cabin pressure, while varying airflow across its planned ventilation range.

What makes it creative

Finding a relevant experiment and finding evidence that covers your scenario are two different steps. Flame Fall lets users explore both in one place. BASS-II shows how acrylic responds to changes in airflow in ISS microgravity. LUCI adds flame-spread measurements from simulated lunar gravity in a shared chamber. Put the studies side by side and you can see what each contributes to the rover question and which combination of conditions still needs a dedicated test.

What we considered

We accounted for sample geometry, airflow protocols, and how gravity was produced or simulated, because each affects how an experiment can inform a new scenario. We kept initial, final, and nominal measurements distinct, preserved original and standardized units, and marked unreported values. Each curated record is traceable to its source, and the catalog is versioned so users can reproduce a comparison.

What we built it with

We used React and TypeScript for the interface, Node.js and Express for the API, Zod for validation, and Python to validate and build the catalog from CSV and JSON. Deterministic rules produce the rankings and coverage checks. Gemini explains those results using curated evidence, with reviewed fallback explanations available when the model is unavailable.

Intended impact

For students, Flame Fall turns a technical report into an experiment they can interrogate. For researchers, it makes a literature search actionable by helping them specify what to test next. We want teams working on materials, ventilation, detection, or suppression to leave with a source they can cite and a concrete question for their next experiment.
